newsitem.title: UK: Brazil seen tightening credit as trade gap soars.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seen tightening credit as trade gap soars.

text.p: Brazil is likely to tighten credit restrictions if its trade position keeps deterioriating and it could also employ administrative measures hampering imports and promoting exports, analysts said.

In a note to investors Kleinwort Benson analyst Neil Dougall said that a faster currency depreciation was less likely, even though speculation has been running rife that Brazil might choose that way of tackling an ugly looking trade deficit.

"A more appropriate policy response -- if the trade position continued to deterioriate -- would be a dampening of consumer demand," he said. "This would most likely come via a tightening of credit restrictions."
He said Brazil might also raise reserve requirements for banks, adding that even a mild credit tightening would yield disproportionately large results.
"A gentle nudge on the tiller is all that is required."

Brazil last week posted what Stephen Rose, of London-based brokerage Stephen Rose and partners, described as the worst monthly trade deficit figure in the country's history -- a whopping $1.3 billion, beyond the most pessimistic expectations.
Brazil's trade account is caught in the pincer of sluggish exports and an import boom fuelled by strong economic growth.

But the government is arguing that the October figure does not signal a trend and that the current account shortfall will amount to a comfortable 3.0 percent of GDP this year, while foreign reserves of $58 billion equal 14 months' import cover.
Some foreign investors, haunted by the memory of the 1994 Mexican crisis, are treating the October trade figure as a trend, producing deficit projections of $4.0 billion for 1996 and $6.0 for 1997.
While the government denies that the economy is overheating, Dougall said the October trade numbers signalled clearly the dangers of allowing demand to race ahead.

Some analysts point to special factors, including oil price rises and a pre-Christmas surge in consumer good imports, as weighing in the October data, while some pump priming ahead of October municipal elections may have boosted economic growth.
But Dougall said that given the fiscal and trade constraints, the government needed to be careful not to let the economy power ahead too fast.
Preliminary figures indicate third quarter year-on-year GDP growth of 7.0 percent. But the government is still predicting an annual figure of 3.0 percent this year, and 4.5 percent in 1997.
"Far better to trim demand growth at an early stage rather than risk a much bigger adjustment later," Dougall said.
He said faster exchange rate depreciation was risky given the reliance on the Real plan as an exchange rate anchor in the absence of fundamental fiscal reform.
Other options include temporary increase in protectionism, but it seemed unlikely given that Brazil is already under World Trade Organisation pressure to hurry along tariff cuts.
And an interest rate rise would be very much a last resort, given its adverse impact on public sector finances, Dougall said.
Stephen Rose agreed that a major depreciation was unlikely.

"We would be very surprised to see a maxi devaluation which would certainly provoke resignations in the economic team... (and) real interest rates are already high enough," he said. But he thought the tariff route possible.

"Our guess is that the Ministry of Finance's reaction to the figures will be a series of minor adjustments affecting the terms of import and export credit, possibly some further export incentives through tax breaks and a few more tariff barriers for imports," he said. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
